fetched_contents.text: Determining Capillary Pore–Size Distribution of Soil from Soil–Water Retention Curve | Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering Publication: Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering Volume 150, Issue 2 Abstract Pore-size distribution (PSD) of soil is a fundamental property that determines flows of water, heat, chemicals, and electricity and controls distributions of stress and deformation. PSD can be intrinsically related to the soil–water retention curve (SWRC), which is a constitutive relationship describing how the soil skeleton retains pore water via adsorption and capillarity. A general framework to quantify soil’s PSD is proposed by first fitting an analytical SWRC model to experimental water retention curves that explicitly separate the SWRC into an adsorptive SWRC and a capillary SWRC. The PSD is then estimated at incremental steps by combining the capillary SWRC and the conventional Young–Laplace equation relating capillary pressure to pore size. Cumulative and density PSD curves for 11 soils covering a wide spectrum of soil types are determined and compared with the PSD functions independently measured using mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP). Good agreement is observed in the estimated pore size range, distribution pattern, and peak position determined from the two different methods. Differences observed in the methods are attributed to differences inherent in the use of wetting and nonwetting fluids to probe the pore space. The SWRC-based method generally characterizes pore sizes ranging from 100 to 0.02 μm with a major peak located within a pore diameter range of 1–10 μm. As the clay content increases, a secondary peak becomes evident at smaller pore sizes (about 0.01–0.1 μm), where the bimodal pattern reflects the dual-porosity microstructure commonly observed for clayey soils. For soils containing swelling clays, PSD can change substantially with variation in water content; thus, the water-based method is more appropriate than MIP for applications to geotechnical engineering practice. fetched_contents.text: Predictive Modeling of Saturated Hydraulic Conductivity using Machine Learning Techniques | Engineering, Technology & Applied Science Research Authors * Moussa S. Elbisy Civil Engineering Department, College of Engineering and Architecture, Umm Al-Qura University, Makkah, Saudi Arabia Received: 13 January 2025 | Revised: 31 January 2025 | Accepted: 5 February 2025 | Online: 16 February 2025 Corresponding author: Moussa S. Elbisy Abstract The hydraulic conductivity of saturated soil is a critical parameter for understanding various engineering challenges related to groundwater. Machine learning techniques offer powerful methods to address complex nonlinear regression problems. This study developed three models, namely a Multilayer Perceptron Neural Network (MPNN), a Support Vector Machine (SVM), and a Tree Boost, to predict field saturated hydraulic conductivity using easily measurable soil properties, such as hydraulic conductivity, clay/silt ratio, soil saturation percentage, d90 of grains, liquid limit, plastic limit, soil pH, hydrocarbon anions, chloride ions, and calcium carbonate content. Soil samples were collected from two locations: the El-Nubaria and Sinai regions, located in the western delta of Egypt. To evaluate the performance of these models, five distinct metrics, namely Mean Squared Error (MSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Scatter Index (SI), and Correlation Coefficient (R), were employed along with a Taylor diagram. Standard laboratory procedures for measuring specific surface area are primarily adsorption-based, with the two broad categories being gas adsorption and polar-liquid adsorption. The evidence explicitly groups methods into these two categories: gas adsorption and adsorption of polar liquids or molecules from solution [N1-R1][N1-R3]. A practical procedure example in the shared evidence also includes grain-size analysis and examination of grain shape characteristics as part of a broader specific-surface-area analysis workflow [N1-R4]. Another search result indicates that specific surface area can be estimated from soil textural data or particle-size distribution, which suggests that empirical estimation is possible when direct adsorption measurements are not feasible [N6-R5]. In plastic soils, this means that specific-surface-area determination can depend heavily on the soil’s fine-grained composition and the availability of particle-size data, since fine-grained soils are more likely to have high surface area and complex pore structure [N6-R5][N6-R2].

Standard laboratory procedures for determining liquid limit are also clearly indicated in the shared evidence. The search results emphasize that surface area and clay content significantly influence Atterberg limits in fine-grained soils, and that empirical relationships link intergrain water at limits to surface area and clay content [N6-R3]. The liquid-limit correlation is also directly tied to clay and plasticity, with the evidence stating that the relationship between liquid limit and specific surface area, cation exchange capacity, and activity of clays has been statistically reappraised [N6-R1]. This means the liquid-limit determination is not just a single measurement but is often interpreted through soil composition, especially in plastic soils where clay content is high. The evidence also suggests that the liquid limit depends on moisture conditions because the Atterberg-limit relationships are tied to intergrain water retention, which is moisture-sensitive [N6-R2][N6-R3].

Both measurements depend strongly on soil composition and moisture conditions. For specific surface area, fine-grained soils and those with high clay content are expected to show higher surface area, which is why particle-size distribution and grain-shape analysis are important parts of the procedure [N1-R4][N6-R5]. For liquid limit, the evidence links the limit to clay content and plasticity, implying that soils with higher clay content or higher plasticity will have different liquid-limit values even for the same particle composition [N6-R1][N6-R3]. Moisture conditions are also relevant because Atterberg-limit behavior is tied to intergrain water, which changes with moisture content [N6-R2][N6-R3]. Overall, the experimental determination of specific surface area and liquid limit is therefore a composition- and moisture-dependent process in plastic soils, where clay content and particle-size distribution are especially important [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

Common model types used for saturated hydraulic conductivity prediction include machine learning techniques, pedotransfer functions (PTFs), and statistical regression models. The shared evidence on predictive modeling reports three machine learning models: Multilayer Perceptron Neural Network (MPNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Tree Boost [N4-F3]. It also notes that Tree Boost demonstrated exceptional accuracy in predicting field-saturated hydraulic conductivity, with the lowest Scatter Index (SI) and highest correlation coefficient (R) among the tested models [N4-F3]. In addition, the evidence explicitly references a generalizable pedotransfer-function approach for saturated hydraulic conductivity using transfer learning and predictor selector algorithms [N4-F3]. This indicates that predictive models can be either data-driven machine learning models or more structured PTF approaches, depending on the available data and the target application.

Model inputs and calibration depend heavily on available soil data. The evidence shows that hydraulic conductivity predictions are built using easily measurable soil properties, including hydraulic conductivity, clay/silt ratio, soil saturation percentage, d90 of grains, liquid limit, plastic limit, soil pH, hydrocarbon anions, chloride ions, and calcium carbonate content [N4-F3]. It also mentions that pedotransfer-function development requires appropriate framing of scale and spatial-temporal accuracy of input parameters, which means the calibration is not only about choosing the right model but also about matching the data to the spatial and temporal context of the problem [N4-R4]. The shared evidence on soil properties and hydraulic conductivity testing further supports that input data include soil composition, classification, and hydraulic conductivity testing methods, reinforcing that predictive modeling relies on a broad soil-property dataset [N5-F4].

What practical gains are expected from including specific surface area and liquid limit? The evidence indicates that specific surface area is empirically estimated using correlations with other available parameters such as liquid limit [N2-R1]. It also shows that liquid limit is strongly linked to clay content and Atterberg-limit behavior in fine-grained soils [N6-R3]. Because hydraulic conductivity is influenced by pore structure, clay content, and moisture conditions, these properties are likely to improve predictive accuracy when they are included in the model inputs. The evidence on pore-size distribution further suggests that hydraulic conductivity is directly connected to particle-size distribution and, by extension, to the physical structure of the soil [N3-R4]. Including specific surface area and liquid limit can therefore add important mechanistic information about the soil’s fine-grained structure and water-retention behavior, which are often missing from simpler models that rely only on grain size or void ratio [N2-R1][N6-R1][N6-R3][N3-R4]. The practical gain is therefore expected to be stronger predictions, particularly in plastic soils where clay content and pore connectivity are critical [N2-R1][N6-R1][N6-R3].

Empirically linked soil properties to saturated hydraulic conductivity include particle-size distribution, clay content, void ratio, porosity, liquid limit, plastic limit, soil saturation, and texture-related parameters. The shared evidence explicitly states that hydraulic conductivity can be estimated using particle-size distribution, bulk density, organic carbon content, and effective porosity, and that particle-size distribution is a fundamental property controlling flows through soil [N2-R5][N3-R4]. It also emphasizes that saturated hydraulic conductivity depends on soil texture and structure, and that soils with large conducting pores have higher saturated hydraulic conductivity [N7-R1]. The evidence further links soil texture to pore size distribution and to saturated hydraulic conductivity, noting that sandy soils with larger pores tend to have higher conductivity than finer-textured soils [N7-R3][N7-R5]. These findings establish that texture, porosity, and pore-size distribution are strong empirical predictors.

Specific surface area and liquid limit compare favorably to other predictors such as clay content and void ratio, but they are not necessarily dominant in all cases. The evidence shows that specific surface area is empirically estimated from other available parameters such as liquid limit [N2-R1], and that liquid limit is strongly linked to clay content and Atterberg-limit behavior in fine-grained soils [N6-R3]. This suggests that specific surface area and liquid limit are derived predictors rather than independent measurements in many empirical models, and that they are especially useful when clay content and fine-grained structure are important. In contrast, void ratio and particle-size distribution are more directly measurable physical properties that control pore space and connectivity [N2-R5][N3-R4]. The evidence indicates that hydraulic conductivity is strongly affected by soil texture and structure, which are broader predictors that include void ratio, particle size, and pore connectivity [N7-R1][N7-R5]. So, in plastic soils, clay content and void ratio remain important, but specific surface area and liquid limit provide added value by capturing fine-grained structure and water-retention behavior [N2-R1][N6-R3][N7-R1][N7-R5].

Correlations are soil-type dependent and vary in strength. The evidence explicitly states that the relationship between liquid limit and specific surface area, cation exchange capacity, and activity of clays has been statistically reappraised [N6-R1], which implies that the strength of the correlation is not universal and can change with soil type. The evidence also notes that pore-size distribution is intrinsically related to the soil-water retention curve and that the water-based method is more appropriate than mercury intrusion porosimetry for geotechnical practice, especially in soils where water content affects pore structure [N3-F2]. This supports the conclusion that correlations are soil-type dependent, especially in clayey or swelling soils. In terms of strength, the evidence indicates that hydraulic conductivity can be estimated directly from particle-size distribution and that the Kozeny–Carman equation can predict saturated hydraulic conductivity when enough information is available [N2-R2][N2-R3]. However, the evidence also shows that empirical relationships are often statistical or indirect, which means the strength of the correlation can be moderate to strong but not perfect [N2-R1][N2-R5]. Overall, the best empirical predictors in plastic soils are likely to be a combination of texture, structure, porosity, and clay-related properties, with specific surface area and liquid limit providing particularly useful indirect indicators of fine-grained behavior [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R3][N7-R1].

Specific surface area affects pore structure and flow resistance by increasing the total surface area available for water retention and altering the physical structure of fine-grained soils. The evidence states that surface area and clay content significantly influence Atterberg limits in fine-grained soils, and that the increase in specific surface area with decreasing particle size enhances the soil’s capacity to retain water [N6-R3]. It also indicates that specific surface area is empirically estimated from other soil properties and that it is linked to clay content and cation exchange capacity [N2-R1][N6-R1]. These findings suggest that specific surface area is not just a surface-area metric but also a structural one, because it reflects the capacity of soil particles to hold water and to create a more complex pore network. In practical terms, higher specific surface area can increase flow resistance by creating more tortuous pathways and more adsorptive surfaces that slow water movement [N6-R3][N2-R1].

Liquid limit relates to clay content and plasticity-driven pore connectivity because it is directly tied to Atterberg-limit behavior and to the activity and cation exchange capacity of clays [N6-R1][N6-R3]. The evidence also notes that surface area and clay content significantly influence Atterberg limits, which are measures of the soil’s water-retention capacity at specific moisture thresholds [N6-R3]. In plastic soils, this means that higher clay content typically leads to higher liquid limits and greater pore connectivity through the formation of fine-grained, adsorptive structures. The evidence on pore-size distribution further supports this by showing that clay content can change the pore-size distribution, producing secondary peaks at smaller pores and affecting the overall pore structure [N3-F2]. Thus, liquid limit is a proxy for the structural and connectivity properties of fine-grained soils, especially in plastic soils where clay activity and plasticity drive pore connectivity [N6-R1][N6-R3][N3-F2].

Together, specific surface area and liquid limit influence saturated hydraulic conductivity by controlling the pore structure and the resistance to water flow. The evidence shows that pore-size distribution is a fundamental property that determines flows of water and controls distributions of stress and deformation [N3-F2]. It also links hydraulic conductivity to particle-size distribution and to the Kozeny–Carman equation, which implies that pore size and structure are central to flow resistance [N2-R2][N2-R3]. In plastic soils, higher specific surface area and higher liquid limit are associated with finer particle size, greater water retention, and more complex pore structure, all of which can reduce saturated hydraulic conductivity by increasing tortuosity and adsorption [N6-R3][N2-R1][N3-F2]. Conversely, soils with lower specific surface area and lower liquid limit tend to have coarser structures and less adsorptive behavior, which can support higher conductivity. Therefore, the combination of specific surface area and liquid limit matters because they jointly capture the fine-grained structural and connectivity features that control how easily water can move through the soil [N2-R1][N6-R1][N6-R3][N3-F2].

In plastic soils, this is especially relevant because fine-grained soils and those with high clay content are expected to show higher surface area, so particle-size data and grain-shape analysis are important parts of the procedure [N6-R5][N6-R2].

The evidence shows that surface area and clay content significantly influence Atterberg limits in fine-grained soils, and that empirical relationships link intergrain water at limits to surface area and clay content [N6-R3]. It also states that the relationship between liquid limit and specific surface area, cation exchange capacity, and activity of clays has been statistically reappraised [N6-R1].
